description: BugHappens is a student team building software to monitor astronaut health during space missions. The idea: collect vital signs from wearable sensors (heart rate, blood oxygen, sleep, stress), use machine learning to flag early warning signs, and keep this sensitive medical data private and secure. We bring electronics, ML and data protection skills. Looking for: a frontend or mobile developer, someone with medical or biology knowledge, and a pitch designer. Bugs happen; we fix them fast.
summary:
On long missions, stress, radiation, disrupted sleep and heavy workloads weaken astronauts' immune systems, and dormant viruses such as the one behind shingles can reactivate. Far from Earth, with communication delays of up to 22 minutes each way near Mars, crews must catch problems early and act on their own.

ORBIT is an onboard immune early-warning system. It learns each astronaut's personal baseline from wearables, daily check-ins and onboard lab tests, detects unusual changes, and turns them into one clear, explainable status (green, yellow, orange or red) with the reasons behind it and concrete procedures, such as taking a saliva sample or informing the crew medical officer.

Astronauts can simply describe how they feel in a chat. ORBIT extracts the symptoms, screens for red flags first, asks a few targeted questions, and produces a report they can correct before saving. It counts real NASA DONKI space-weather events as immune stressors, keeps private health data onboard unless the astronaut consents to share it, and runs fully offline.
details:
What it does
ORBIT gives every astronaut a daily answer to three questions: Am I OK? Why? What do I do? It combines wearable data (skin temperature, heart rate and its variability, breathing rate, sleep), a daily check-in, onboard lab tests (saliva viral DNA, CRP) and mission events (spacewalks, real solar storms) into one explainable status, with step-by-step procedures. It has five screens:

  • Chat: describe symptoms in plain words, answer a few questions, and correct the report before saving.
  • Today: your level, the reasons and what to do now, plus trends and a mission replay.
  • Quick check-in: a 60-second form.
  • Crew: a view for the commander and the medical officer, showing only what each astronaut shares.
  • Earth: a consent-based report to mission control, sent over a realistic Moon or Mars delay.

How it works

  • Personal baselines. Each signal is compared with the astronaut’s own normal (a 14-day rolling median), not a population average.
  • Anomaly detection. Robust statistics flag both sudden spikes and slow multi-day drifts.
  • Explainable scoring. A 0–100 score where every point has a reason, for example “Skin temperature 0.45 °C above your normal for 2 days, +9”, and the dashboard shows what the score would be without each reason.
  • Symptom chat. A red-flag check runs before any model, so urgent symptoms such as trouble breathing or chest pain go straight to “Get medical help now”. An extractor then finds symptoms, severity and negations (“no rash, but a burning patch”). A reasoner ranks 8 possible patterns and asks the single most informative next question. Results show as likely or possible, never as a diagnosis.
    • The learned scorer warned earlier (24 of 45 illnesses before symptom day, against 16 for the rules) with no extra false alarms.
    • The Bayesian reasoner was far better calibrated (Brier score 0.04 against 0.19) and needed 1.5 questions instead of 3.6.

NASA data and resources

  • Real NASA DONKI data. ORBIT reads real space-weather events from NASA’s DONKI database through the NASA Open APIs. It models a real mission: the ground fetches the data, the spacecraft reads a local cache offline, and real solar particle events and geomagnetic storms become crew-wide stressors in the score.
  • NASA research. The design builds on NASA research on immune dysregulation and herpesvirus reactivation in astronauts. That research is why ORBIT watches VZV, HSV-1 and EBV, and why its first procedure is a saliva viral-DNA test.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Earlier warning, while symptoms are still mild and countermeasures (rest, workload changes, testing) work best.
  • Crew autonomy: clear, trustworthy guidance onboard, without waiting for Earth.
  • Less burden on the medical officer, and a structured record of symptoms for the flight surgeon.
  • Potential use on Earth: the same approach could serve people in isolated or extreme settings, such as polar stations, submarines and remote work.

Tools and technologies
Python 3.11, FastAPI, Pydantic v2, SQLite and pandas for the backend; scikit-learn for training only (trained weights are stored as readable JSON); React 19, TypeScript, Vite and Recharts for the frontend; pytest (607 automated tests); GitHub Actions, GitHub Pages and Render for deployment; the NASA DONKI API. We used AI coding assistants to help write and review code, tests and documentation, as disclosed in the README.

What makes it creative

  • Chat-first check-in. Astronauts talk instead of filling in forms, and still review what is saved.
  • Real NASA space weather replayed onto a future mission, fetched on the ground and read offline onboard, like a real uplink.
  • Explainability everywhere: every point in the score has a reason, and you can see the score without it.
  • Swappable modules, so rule-based and machine-learning versions can be compared honestly on the same data before switching.

Factors we considered
Safety first (red flags before any model; patterns are never a diagnosis); privacy and consent (nothing leaves the spacecraft without permission); offline operation and communication delays; explainability and trust; accessibility (levels shown by colour and word, keyboard navigation, readable in a dim cabin); honest evaluation on held-out data. Limitations: the health data is simulated, the medical content is illustrative and not clinically validated, and the chat is English-only. code repo: https://github.com/rdenis03/spacemontoringsoftware
